model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Breakthrough on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], color: str) -> tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your pieces. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's pieces. - `color` is `'b'` for black which moves downwards (to lower row values) and `'w'` for white which moves upwards (to higher row values). - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..7`. - Row 0 is the bottom (home row for white); row 7 is the top (home row for black). # Action / Return Format - Return a move as a tuple: `((from_row, from_col), (to_row, to_col))`. - Movement rules: - - A piece may move one space straight forward if the target square is empty. - - A piece may move one space diagonally forward if the target square is empty. - - A piece may capture only by moving one space diagonally forward onto an opponent piece; the opponent piece is removed. - - Capturing is not compulsory and is never chained; you can capture at most one piece per turn. - Win conditions: - - A piece may not move one space straight forward if the target square is not empty (capturing by going forward is not allowed). - - You win immediately if any of your pieces reaches the opponent's home row (furthest row from you). - - You win if all opponent pieces are captured. - - Draws do not occur in Breakthrough. - Your move must be legal. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning a Breakthrough AI using alpha-beta search with iterative deepening within a 1-second limit, making sure it always returns a legal move. I'm working through move generation, win detection, and an evaluation function weighing material, advancement, and piece safety.

I'm settling on a board representation as a flat 64-entry list with 0 for empty, 1 for white, and -1 for black, plus a side-to-move flag. For the evaluation function, I'm considering material count, positional advancement toward the goal row, and detecting "unstoppable runners" that no opponent piece can intercept.

I'm working out the geometry for interception: since pieces only move forward diagonally to capture, a runner is unstoppable if no opponent piece lies within the diagonal cone ahead of it (row and column distance constraints), and any opponent piece already behind it can never catch up since pieces can't move backwards.

I'll be conservative in flagging pieces unstoppable to avoid false positives, giving eval bonuses scaled by remaining distance to promotion, while also factoring in tempo when both sides have runners racing forward. Beyond that, I want the evaluation to penalize any piece that's attacked and left undefended.

I'm also thinking about rewarding home-row occupation for defensive stability early on, and giving credit to pieces that are protected by a friendly piece diagonally behind them. For the actual scoring, I'll assign each piece a base value plus a row-based advancement table that ramps up sharply near promotion, since the search itself will catch immediate wins.

For performance, I'm planning negamax with alpha-beta and iterative deepening, possibly a Zobrist-based transposition table, aiming for depth 4-5 given Python's likely 20-50k nodes/sec throughput. Move generation will scan the flat board array for each side's pieces and check forward and diagonal squares for empty or capturable cells, with terminal checks for reaching the goal row or eliminating the opponent's pieces.

I should also consider stalemate cases where a player has no legal moves — rare but possible if all pieces are blocked. If that happens I'll just fall back to returning the evaluation score, and at the root I'll ensure some move is always returned even if none seem legal, to avoid disqualification. For time management, I'll track elapsed time with periodic node checks and budget roughly 0.75 seconds per move.

I'll use iterative deepening, keeping the best move from the last fully completed depth if time runs out mid-search, unless a forced win was already found. For move ordering, I'll prioritize captures and advancing moves, plus a transposition table using incremental Zobrist hashing for speed rather than hashing the whole board each time.

Setting up the Zobrist hashing and search constants...

Still writing search logic...

I need to track piece counts for both sides to detect a win-by-elimination, so I'll pass those as parameters rather than globals. I'm also weighing whether to add a captures-only quiescence search at the leaf nodes, capped at a few plies with stand-pat evaluation, since capture sequences in Breakthrough are naturally bounded.

I also want the evaluation function to detect immediate win threats: if a piece is one row from the goal with a clear path, that should register as a decisive advantage for whichever side controls it, since the alternating search will otherwise need extra depth to see it.

So I'll evaluate: if the side to move has a piece on the penultimate row, that's essentially a won position; if the opponent has one that can't be captured, that's essentially lost. I'm now working out a per-piece advancement scoring table giving increasing value the closer a piece gets to promotion.

I'm also adding protection bonuses for supported pieces and penalties for hanging pieces under attack, mirroring the logic for black by flipping rows, plus a bonus for having a clear, unstoppable path to promotion where no enemy piece can intercept.

I should widen the cone slightly since black could sidestep diagonally to intercept, so I'll use |cb-c| <= rb-r+1 as a safer bound. For move ordering I'll prioritize captures and advancement toward the goal row, then fall back to a transposition table keyed by position hash including side-to-move, storing depth, score, flag, and best move.

For iterative deepening, I'll loop over increasing depths at the root, reordering moves by previous iteration scores, and rely on a timeout exception to bail out cleanly.

I'm writing the evaluation function that scores material and positional advancement, checking whether each pawn is attacked diagonally by an opponent and whether it's defended, adjusting the score accordingly and giving bonuses for reaching the back rank.

I'm now thinking about how to compute attacker/defender squares efficiently using bit offsets from each piece's index, and considering limiting the more expensive "runner" check (which detects unblockable advancing pawns) to only pieces that have already advanced past midboard, to keep the per-leaf evaluation cost manageable.

For the penultimate-row logic, I'm reasoning through move ordering: if it's white's turn and white has an uncapturable piece on row 6, white wins immediately; otherwise I need to check whether black can capture it before checking if black has its own winning threat on row 1, since whoever moves first with an unstoppable advance should win.

With multiple opponent threats on the penultimate row, a single capture can't stop both, so that's a loss; one uncapturable threat is also a loss, while a capturable one just gets penalized and left for quiescence to resolve. I'm writing the quiescence search function that keeps extending capture sequences at the search horizon, checking for immediate wins and standing pat evaluations along the way.

Immediate wins are already caught by the evaluation function, so I don't need separate handling for goal-row moves. I'll cap quiescence depth around 4 and use a conservative 0.7s time budget with periodic checks every 512 nodes to stay safe against slower CPUs, and I need a fallback that returns a reasonable legal move (prioritizing captures or wins) if the search fails or times out.

Now I'm setting up Zobrist hashing tables, time constants, and positional advancement bonuses by row for each side, plus a custom timeout exception to bail out of search cleanly.

Writing move generation logic...

Simplifying move ordering to just captures-first with TT move prioritized, adding a lightweight history heuristic to break ties among quiet moves. Now sketching the negamax search function signature with alpha-beta pruning.

Writing search function...

Still writing negamax logic...

I'm also noting a subtlety: mate scores stored in the transposition table need ply adjustments when retrieved, otherwise cached mate distances can be wrong when reused at a different search depth from root.

Now I'm sketching the quiescence search — it stands pat with a static evaluation, cuts off if that already beats beta or hits a large mate-range value, then generates and searches capturing moves to resolve tactical sequences before returning a stable score.

I want to make the win/loss scoring ply-aware so the search prefers faster mates rather than treating static evaluation's win detection the same as an actual forced win found deeper in the tree. I'll pass ply into evaluate so a detected win returns WIN - ply - 1, keeping it consistent with how the search scores real checkmates.

For the evaluation function itself, I'm scanning the board to track piece values, positional advancement bonuses, and vulnerability -- checking if pieces are attacked and undefended to penalize exposed pieces accordingly.

Then I'm reasoning through the immediate win/loss detection: if white has a piece on row 6, I need to verify it can always advance to row 7 next turn since the diagonal squares can't be blocked by white pieces (that would mean the game already ended), so this is always a forced win. I'm working out similar logic for black threats near promotion.

If a runner is unopposed and unable to be blocked given the column distance, I should give it an increasing bonus by row, and actually at row 5 with white to move it's essentially a forced win since nothing can stop it from reaching row 6.

I'll set up mirrored scoring for black's runners too, then combine everything into a final evaluation that returns the white-minus-black score, negated when the side to move is black. I'm now sketching out the root policy function, starting with the board setup and side-to-move handling.

Still writing policy...

Since depth-1 always finishes before timeout, that iteration's result is safe to rely on. I need piece counts (wc, bc) to detect the "captured all opponent pieces" win condition after each capture. For the no-legal-moves edge case, I'll just return the static evaluation rather than a forced win/loss, since it's ambiguous and rare. For move ordering history heuristics, I'll use a flat 64x64 list instead of a dict for speed.

I'm writing an ordering function that scores moves: TT move first, captures next, then history heuristic values, with promotion-to-goal-row moves boosted even higher since they win immediately. Rough performance estimate is 15-30k nodes/sec in pure Python with this evaluation function.

Depth 4-5 plus quiescence should be workable. Iterating all 64 squares per leaf evaluation with early skips seems fine rather than maintaining separate piece lists.

I'm also reconsidering the hanging-piece penalty since quiescence already resolves captures for the side to move -- a piece hanging for the side about to move is less urgent since they can just move it, while a piece hanging for the opponent gets caught by quiescence anyway. So I should probably scale down the penalties from 35/15 to something like 25/10.

I should also add a small bonus for pieces being defended, plus consider penalizing advanced pieces that lack support, and sharpen the penalty for opponent pieces that get deep into friendly territory since those are close to threatening a win.

Setting up Zobrist hashing, time budget constants, and advancement/breakthrough-run value tables for the search...

Adding transposition table and history heuristic storage, then writing a function to generate capture moves for pawns diagonally forward on the board for each side.

Now I'm building the evaluation function, scoring material and positional factors like advancement bonuses, attack/defense status for hanging pieces, and promotion proximity for both white and black pawns.

I'm also checking for immediate win conditions and threats: white winning if it has a piece on rank 6 poised to promote, black winning if it has two pieces on rank 1, and handling the single-threat case by checking whether that piece is capturable before adjusting the score.

I mirror the same logic for black's runners, checking each advanced white pawn for a clear path with no black blockers within capturing range, then apply the corresponding bonus. After computing both sides' scores I return the net score, flipped depending on whose turn it is—though I'm second-guessing whether treating a single capturable black threat as just a scoring bonus is really correct, since it might actually need deeper search to confirm white can safely capture.

I'm also double-checking the quiescence search's stand-pat evaluation and confirming that the penultimate-row logic works correctly even when it's not the advanced pawn's side to move. Then I move to structuring the negamax search, deciding root-level move handling needs separate treatment since a transposition table hit at depth 0 shouldn't short-circuit before a move is chosen.

Writing root search function...

After undoing the move, I record each move's score and track the best one, then sort all moves by descending score so the next iteration explores the most promising moves first.

I'm also flagging a subtlety: since alpha gets updated at the root, scores for moves other than the best are really just upper bounds from fail-low searches, which is fine for move ordering purposes. There's a deeper concern about transposition table entries storing mate scores relative to ply depth—the same position reached at different depths could get mismatched scores, which is a minor correctness issue I'm choosing to set aside for now rather than fix immediately.

I'm also confirming that the game can't loop into infinite repetition since pieces only advance forward, so games are guaranteed to terminate, and I need to account for a roughly 0.72 second time budget when structuring the search.

Since the exact clock speed of the arena is unknown, I'll drop the safety margin down to around 0.65 seconds and check node counts every 256 nodes for fine-grained timing control, which should still keep recursion depth manageable alongside quiescence search. I'm also verifying the move generation logic for white pawns handles edge columns correctly to avoid wrapping errors.

Now I'm working out move ordering for negamax, avoiding lambdas in favor of computing a numeric key directly for each move -- giving the transposition table move the highest priority, then promotions, then captures scored by the captured piece's value, and finally falling back to history heuristic scores for quiet moves, sorted in descending order.

I want to double-check that immediate win detection is consistent: the score formula WIN - ply - 1 should line up between negamax and the evaluation function, since the winning move occurs at the current ply. I also want to verify the transposition table lookup happens before quiescence search when depth is zero, and think through whether the evaluation function's board scoring handles all cases correctly.

Let me reconsider the attack-detection logic — I'm using nested if/elif branches to check diagonal captures, and I need to make sure the elif doesn't skip a valid attack check when the first condition fails.

Now I'll wrap the whole search in a try/except that falls back gracefully on any exception, then write out the complete final code.
